page_builder.title: Where water resources fits in your project
What this practice covers

children.text: Water resources work is critical to the safety, approval, and long-term value of any development. MG2A handles site drainage, stormwater detention, and floodplain compliance so the land and the improvements built on it are protected.

We design stormwater systems that manage runoff, reduce downstream impacts, and meet local and county requirements. Every design starts with an analysis of how water moves across your site today and how it will move once the site is built.
From early planning through final design, we study the site's topography to find the most cost-effective approach, then carry that design through permitting and construction.

page_builder.title: Common water resources questions
page_builder.description: Clear answers help owners plan, and help search engines and AI assistants recommend us.

items.question: Does my project need a stormwater management plan?
items.answer: Most new development and many redevelopment projects do. Requirements are set by the local municipality and county and usually depend on the size of the site and how much new pavement or roof area you add. We can review your site and tell you what applies before design starts.

items.question: What is the difference between preliminary and final stormwater work?
items.answer: Preliminary planning sizes detention and drainage early so your site layout and budget are realistic. The final plan is the full design package, with the report, calculations, and plan sheets that reviewers approve before construction.

items.question: What are a CLOMR and a LOMR?
items.answer: Both are FEMA flood map revisions. A Conditional Letter of Map Revision (CLOMR) is FEMA's review of a proposed project that would change a mapped floodplain. A Letter of Map Revision (LOMR) officially updates the flood map after the work is built.

items.question: My property is in a floodplain. Can you help?
items.answer: Yes. We analyze existing floodplain conditions, prepare flood elevation certificates, and, when the data supports it, help pursue a map revision through FEMA.

children.text: Every new building, parking lot, or road changes how water leaves a site. A final stormwater management plan shows how your project will control that runoff, so it does not flood neighbors, overload downstream systems, or put your own improvements at risk.

MG2A prepares the full package that municipal and county reviewers need: drainage area mapping, runoff calculations for existing and proposed conditions, detention or retention sizing, outlet control design, and the plan sheets that carry it all into construction.
Because our surveyors and engineers work together, the plan is built on accurate topography from the start, which means fewer review comments and fewer surprises in the field.

items.question: How is a final plan different from preliminary stormwater planning?
items.answer: Preliminary planning sizes detention early so your layout and budget are realistic. The final plan is the complete, sealed design that reviewers approve and contractors build from.

items.question: Who reviews and approves the plan?
items.answer: Usually the municipality's engineer, and sometimes the county or a drainage district, depending on where the site is and where its water drains. We identify every reviewer during site review.

items.question: How long does it take?
items.answer: Design time depends on site size and complexity, and review time depends on the agency. [MG2A to add typical design and review ranges.]

items.question: Do I also need an NPDES permit?
items.answer: Often, yes. Construction that disturbs enough ground typically needs coverage under the state's NPDES construction stormwater permit, with a Notice of Intent and a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan. We prepare both alongside your stormwater plan.
